overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing Chapter One — the Boundaries of Temurah
overview.subtitle: Temurah 13a–13b
overview.hebrewSource: יָחִיד עוֹשֶׂה תְּמוּרָה, וְאֵין הַצִּבּוּר וְהַשּׁוּתָּפִין עוֹשִׂין תְּמוּרָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara supplies verse sources for the mishna's rules that a substitute cannot itself generate a further substitute, and that an animal's offspring cannot become one either (Rabbi Yehuda dissents on the latter). A new mishna then draws the outer boundaries of temurah altogether: birds and meal offerings cannot generate substitutes (the verse says only 'animal'), nor can animals owned by the community or by partners, nor items consecrated for Temple maintenance (bedek habayit) — only an individual's own altar-offering can. The Gemara traces each exclusion to its verse, debates whether bedek habayit even counts as a 'korban,' and explores the special double substitution unique to the animal tithe (temurat shmo vs. temurat gufo). The daf — and the chapter — closes with a question about whether a voluntary burnt offering counts as an 'obligatory' offering for purposes of temurah.

slides.title: 📜 Two Rules, Two Verses
slides.subtitle: Both drawn from the same phrase in Leviticus 27:10
rows: A substitute cannot generate a further substitute
'וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' — its substitute, not the substitute of its substitute
An offspring cannot become a substitute
'הוּא' — it (the consecrated animal itself), not its offspring
Disagrees: 'יִהְיֶה' (shall be) includes the offspring too
Includes one who substitutes unwittingly — treated as if intentional

callout.label: Pattern:
callout.text: Every boundary of temurah in this tractate traces back to a specific word in the same verse, read narrowly by some and expansively by others.

slides.title: 🕊️ New Mishna: Who and What CAN'T Make a Substitute
slides.subtitle: Only an individual's own altar-offering generates temurah

boxes.title: Cannot Make Temurah
items: Birds (doves/pigeons) — verse says only 'בְּהֵמָה,' an animal
Community-owned animals — 'לֹא יַחֲלִיפֶנּוּ' implies a single, individual owner

boxes.title: CAN Make Temurah
items: Rabbi Shimon's proof: the animal tithe (מַעֲשֵׂר) models the pattern — individual, altar-bound, obligatory, not in partnership

callout.label: Rabbi Shimon's method:
callout.text: Since the animal tithe is singled out for its own substitution verse, its four traits (individual/altar/obligatory/non-partnership) define exactly which offerings the general rule covers.

slides.title: ❓ Is Bedek HaBayit Called a 'Korban'?
slides.subtitle: Two baraitot seem to contradict each other

lines.speaker: Baraita 1
lines.text: 'קׇרְבָּן' in the temurah verse refers only to what is CALLED a korban — excluding bedek habayit, which is not called a korban.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But another baraita treats bedek habayit AS a korban — deriving from 'entrance of the Tent of Meeting' that only items fit for the altar are excluded from the offering-outside-Temple prohibition, implying bedek habayit otherwise would count!

lines.speaker: Rabbi Ḥanina resolves
lines.text: No contradiction: the first baraita follows the Rabbis (bedek habayit is NOT called korban); the second follows Rabbi Shimon (it IS called korban, though excluded from temurah via the ma'aser juxtaposition instead).

lines.speaker: Further precision
lines.text: Even for the Rabbis, bedek habayit IS called 'the Lord's offering' (קׇרְבַּן ה'), just never 'an offering TO the Lord' (קׇרְבָּן לַה') — the phrase reserved for altar offerings.

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: Whether bedek habayit is excluded from temurah by the word 'korban' or by analogy to the animal tithe depends entirely on which tanna you follow.

slides.title: 🔀 The Animal Tithe's Double Substitution
slides.subtitle: Temurat Shmo (substitute of its name) vs. Temurat Gufo (substitute of its body)
rows: No — only on a fit animal
Yes — even on an unfit one

callout.label: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's point:
callout.text: Since 'temurat shmo' (a counting error making the 10th and 11th animals both sacred) is unique to the tithe, the Torah had to separately confirm that ordinary temurah (temurat gufo) applies to the tithe too.

slides.title: 💰 Does a Voluntary Burnt Offering Count as 'Obligatory'?
slides.subtitle: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak challenges Rava on Rabbi Shimon's requirement

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Shimon requires temurah-eligible offerings to be 'דָּבָר שֶׁבָּא בְּחוֹבָה' — something obligatory. Does that exclude a voluntary burnt offering?
2️⃣ Rava: no — once a person accepts a voluntary offering upon himself, it becomes his personal obligation, and DOES generate temurah
3️⃣ What Rabbi Shimon's rule really excludes: a burnt offering purchased from LEFTOVER funds (e.g., money remaining after buying a sin/guilt offering)

4️⃣ This connects back to Rabbi Avin's earlier unresolved dilemma (9b–10a): does repeat substitution work on an animal now reclassified via leftover funds? Depends on whose position (R' Eliezer vs. R' Shimon) applies — left as an open question (תִּיבְּעֵי)

callout.label: Chapter ends here:
callout.text: הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ הַכֹּל מְמִירִין — 'We will return to you, [chapter] Everyone Substitutes.' This marks the close of the tractate's first chapter.

summary.principle: Temurah is bounded on every side by the verse's precise language: only an individual's own altar-bound, obligatory offering — not a bird, meal offering, communal or partnership animal, or bedek habayit item — generates a substitute, and never a substitute of a substitute.

flowSteps.content: 📜 'וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' bars substitute-of-substitute; 'הוּא' bars offspring (R' Yehuda dissents on offspring)
🕊️ New mishna: birds, meal offerings, communal/partnership animals, and bedek habayit are all excluded

columns.content: ❓ Whether bedek habayit is 'korban' splits Rabbis and R' Shimon
🔀 The tithe alone has BOTH temurat shmo and temurat gufo

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: temurah applies only to what the animal tithe models — individual, altar-bound, obligatory, non-partnership offerings

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, what verse phrase teaches that a substitute animal cannot itself generate a further substitute?
o: 'הוּא' (it)
'וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' — 'its substitute,' not the substitute of its substitute
'קָרְבָּנוֹ' (his offering)
'לֹא יְבַקֵּר'
quiz.e: The Gemara reads 'וּתְמוּרָתוֹ' (and its substitute) as limiting the halakha to the original consecrated animal's substitute, excluding any further chain of substitution.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, which of the following can generate a valid temurah?
o: A dove brought as an offering
A meal offering
An animal owned by a community or by partners
An individual's own animal offering brought to the altar
quiz.e: The mishna limits temurah to an individual's own altar-bound animal offering; birds, meal offerings, and communal/partnership animals are all explicitly excluded.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Ḥanina resolve the apparent contradiction between two baraitot over whether bedek habayit is called a 'korban'?
o: He says one baraita is simply mistaken
He attributes them to different tannaim — the Rabbis (not called korban) and Rabbi Shimon (called korban, excluded instead via the animal tithe analogy)
He says bedek habayit is never mentioned in either baraita
He merges them into one opinion
quiz.e: Rabbi Ḥanina explains that the baraita excluding bedek habayit via the word 'korban' follows the Rabbis, while the baraita treating it as a korban follows Rabbi Shimon, who instead derives its exclusion from the animal-tithe juxtaposition.

quiz.q: What is one key difference between temurat shmo (substitute of the tithe's name) and temurat gufo (ordinary substitute)?
o: There is no difference between them
Temurat shmo is sacrificed on the altar as a peace offering and can be redeemed if blemished; temurat gufo is never sacrificed and is never redeemed
Temurat gufo is always more stringent in every way
Temurat shmo only applies to birds
quiz.e: Temurat shmo (from a counting error) is treated like a regular peace offering — sacrificed if fit, redeemed if blemished — while temurat gufo (ordinary substitution of the tithe) is never sacrificed and can never be redeemed.

quiz.q: According to Rava, why does a voluntary burnt offering still generate temurah despite Rabbi Shimon's requirement that the offering be 'obligatory' (davar sheba chovah)?
o: Rabbi Shimon's requirement doesn't really exist
Once a person accepts the voluntary offering upon himself, it becomes his personal obligation
Voluntary offerings never generate temurah under any view
It applies only to communal offerings
quiz.e: Rava explains that accepting a voluntary offering makes it obligatory for that individual, satisfying Rabbi Shimon's requirement — what the requirement truly excludes is a burnt offering purchased from leftover consecration funds.
